newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish army bides time in anti-Islamist push.
newsitem.headline: Turkish army bides time in anti-Islamist push.

text.p: Turkey's secularist generals bided their time on Monday in a push against the ruling Islamists that has shaken Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's coalition.

The military-dominated National Security Council (NSC) said in a statement it debated the Kurdish problem and foreign affairs, but it did not discuss army demands for curbs on Islamist revivalism at a four-hour meeting attended by Erbakan.

Turkey's press said on Monday the armed forces would prepare a report in the coming weeks on whether the government is complying with army orders for a return to the rigid secularism of the Turkish republic's early days in the 1920s.

"The report will be put forward at the NSC's April meeting," the Milliyet daily said. Istanbul stocks jumped 3.93 percent on Monday on positive sentiment that the row between the army and government had been put off for the moment.
An NSC call in February to keep Islam out of public life has exposed cracks in Erbakan's alliance with the pro-Western True Path Party.
A True Path minister was quoted on Monday proposing to break up the coalition and to replace it with a secularist team.

"This government cannot find a solution to the tension in the country. A new, broad-based government must be formed without wasting any time," the Hurriyet daily quoted Industry Minister Yalim Erez as saying.
Erez and his party colleagues have become increasingly critical of what they see as Erbakan's reluctance to implement the army's demands.
The generals want to see a cut in the number of "Imam Hatip" Islamic secondary schools, enforcement of a ban on Islamic dress and an assault on pro-Islamist media and business.
Erbakan, the first Islamist to lead NATO-member Turkey, has agreed to the demands in principle but his government has yet to expedite any of them.
The army has deposed three civilian leaders since 1960. A military source told Reuters the army was angered by a bid by Erbakan to introduce mild Islamist reforms.
"The political developments are taking Turkey backwards every day," he said. But he ruled out any coup.

"It has been seen that military administrations don't solve anything," the source said. Analysts say the generals may try to force more True Path MPs to rebel against the coalition if Erbakan does not toe the line.
The True Path, headed by Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, has close ties to the security establishment.
Health Minister Yildirim Aktuna, a True Path member, on Monday repeated doubts he voiced last week on the future of the alliance, Anatolian news agency said.

Erbakan has also faced a backlash from the secularist majority. Almost 10,000 people chanted "Turkey is secularist and will stay that way," at a classical music concert in Ankara attended by the president on Sunday.
